newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban offensive against rebel Masood stalls.
newsitem.headline: Taleban offensive against rebel Masood stalls.

text.p: A Taleban offensive against the valley stronghold of Ahmad Shah Masood stalled on Monday after running into resistance from Afghanistan's ousted military chief a few hundred metres (yards) into the gorge.

Masood forces, making use of native knowledge of the rocky mountain range spanning the steep valley, shelled Taleban positions near the entrance to the gorge and the few fighters manning frontline peaks alongside the valley.

"The main objective now is to take that mountain where the shooting is coming from," said one fighter, pointing to a peak several km (miles) away sprouting occasional plumes of smoke and dust from Taleban tank shells.

The Taleban launched its offensive on the gorge on Saturday, a week after taking over the capital Kabul in a lightning strike that swept Masood and his political mentor President Burhanuddin Rabbani from power.

But after claiming initial gains -- including two mountains overlooking the entrance to the gorge -- the Taleban have encountered sporadic but well-aimed resistance, raining shells on reinforcements gathering at the foot of the mountain range.

Bulldozers were seen entering the valley on Monday to clear mines and landslides triggered ahead of Masood's retreat, but witnesses said the Taleban fighters above and in the valley had advanced only a few hundred metres (yards).

Masood forces appeared to occupy hills some 800 metres (yards) away, a little over one kilometre (half-a-mile) into the 150 km (100 mile) long valley, and on the road around one of the corners of the winding valley floor.

Some locals rejected Taleban claims that it had taken by force the two hills it now occupies, saying the locally born Masood had complied with their requests to withdraw for fear of shelling civilians or the town of Golbahar at the gorge's mouth.
In the town, which straddles the rocky Panjsher river, streets nearest the valley were largely deserted, with only a handful of shops open.
Old people and children wandered the dusty main street, sidestepping mounds of shell casings and jeeps loaded with Taleban fighters that whizzed past.
Military analysts have questioned whether the Taleban are capable of taking the valley, which Masood successfully defended against Soviet firepower in the 1980s.

The British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) earlier quoted a statement issued by warlord General Abdul Rashid Dostum, who holds areas west of the Panjsher, that he would "defend any compatriot" attacked by the Taleban, apparently threatening the Islamic militia with retaliation if they kept attacking Masood.

Masood and Dostum, who have forged uneasy alliances in the past, are the only armies not won over or conquered by the Taleban, who have begun to impose their own fundamentalist brand of Islam on Kabul and areas under their control.
The Taleban came under fire on Sunday as rockets and mortars rained on forces gathering for a second assault on mountains overlooking the valley, sending fighters running for cover.
Monday was quieter, although Masood mortar fire kept Taleban fighters and artillery under cover for much of the day.

Taleban fighters on the front line above the gorge took cover as Masood bombarded the part of the gorge under its control. The Taleban retaliated with a Soviet-made Mi-24 helicopter gunship which fired rockets at Masood positions inside the valley.
"We are just waiting for orders," said one Taleban fighter at the entrance to the gorge around midday.
Another said the offensive would restart on Monday night, echoing earlier promises of an assault on Sunday night that did not materialise. "The elders are still talking," he said.
This offensive has been the first serious warfare since the Taleban took over the capital Kabul in late September, which itself fell with little resistance from Rabbani's forces.
The Taleban have in two years emerged from obscurity as religious students on the Pakistan border in the south to capture three quarters of the country.

Some people in Kabul have welcomed their victory as an end to years of factional warfare but others have been critical of their strict Islamic code which limits the role of women and demands that men pray five times a day.
Only Masood, Rabbani's top commander until the two were ousted from power on September 27, and Dostum control areas outside the Taleban's grip, both of them in the north of the country.
But commanders of the purist Islamic army said they were confident of victory.
